opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing we do is try not to assume anything. With every new DeepSeek release, the team has introduced something architecturally new, whether that's MLA, a new MoE routing scheme, multi-token prediction, or a new sparse attention design. So when we hear a new version is coming, we start by asking which parts we can reuse and which parts are really new.

I think of the work in roughly three layers.

**Model definition and correctness.** We have to implement the model faithfully in SGLang: the attention variant, the expert layout, normalization details, how the weights are sharded and quantized. This is where most of the risk is. If you get a small detail wrong, the model still runs and produces fluent text, but accuracy drops a few points. So a big part of the job is building the evaluation pipeline in parallel and checking against the reference outputs layer by layer.

**Kernels.** If the architecture introduces a new attention pattern, or a new low-precision format like FP8 or FP4 with a different scaling scheme, the existing kernels might not cover it, or might cover it slowly. Often we need new kernels, or need to adapt work from the community, FlashInfer, the DeepSeek open-source kernels, and tune them for Hopper and Blackwell, and increasingly for AMD and other hardware too.

**System-level serving.** A model this large isn't served on one GPU. You need expert parallelism, prefill-decode disaggregation, good data-parallel attention, speculative decoding if there's an MTP head, and all of it has to work together at scale. Day-0 doesn't just mean "it loads." It means people can actually deploy it with reasonable throughput and latency.

So in terms of effort, it's not one person for a weekend. It's a coordinated sprint across our core contributors and partners, often working very closely with the model team before release so we're not starting from zero when the weights drop. The good news is that because we've supported every DeepSeek generation, a lot of the infrastructure, like the MoE and EP machinery, is mature. That lets us focus most of our energy on whatever is truly new in v4.

And I'd say the hardest part isn't any single piece of code. It's the timing. You're trying to be correct, fast, and ready the moment the model is public, and those three goals pull against each other. Our philosophy is correctness first, then a reasonably optimized version on day zero, and then we keep pushing performance over the following weeks.

r001.rationale: The response says each DeepSeek generation introduces architectural novelties and describes implementing new model details, kernels, and serving support as the work required for Day-0 readiness.

r002.rationale: It does not say most implementation code had to be rewritten. It instead says existing infrastructure is mature and the team can reuse it while focusing on what is new.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that Day-0 support is mostly not about the day itself. It's about everything you've done in the months before.

For DeepSeek v4 specifically, the workload breaks into a few pieces. First, the architecture. DeepSeek has consistently shipped things that don't fit the standard dense transformer template: multi-head latent attention, very large fine-grained MoE with shared experts, multi-token prediction heads, and now in v4 the sparse attention and indexer pieces. Each of those touches the inference engine at a different layer. MLA changes how you lay out the KV cache. Fine-grained MoE changes your expert-parallel routing and your kernels. Sparse attention changes your scheduler assumptions about what a decode step even costs. So "support" isn't one PR, it's coordinated changes in the model definition, the attention backend, the memory manager, and the parallelism layer.

Second, the numerics. The weights come in FP8, and some pieces want to stay FP8 end to end while others need to be upcast or re-quantized. Getting the model to produce tokens is easy. Getting it to produce the same tokens as the reference implementation, within tolerance, is where the time actually goes. We spend a lot of effort on correctness harnesses that compare logits layer by layer against a reference.

Third, performance at Day-0 versus Day-30. Realistically, Day-0 means the model runs correctly and reasonably fast on the hardware people actually have, which for most of the community is H100 or H200 nodes, with Blackwell coming online. The fused kernels, the DeepEP-style communication overlap, the speculative decoding with the MTP head, those typically land over the following weeks. We try to be upfront about that distinction.

The way we make Day-0 possible is through early access and co-design. If the first time you see the architecture is the public release, you're already a week behind. The cases where we've shipped same-day support are the ones where we'd been talking with the model team for weeks, had test checkpoints, and had the code mostly ready behind a flag. So I'd say the work is maybe twenty percent on release day and eighty percent before it, and the hard part is building the kind of relationship and abstraction layers that make the twenty percent feasible.

r001.rationale: The response links the workload to DeepSeek v4’s architectural innovations, explaining how MLA, fine-grained MoE, sparse attention, and the indexer require changes across inference-engine layers.

r002.rationale: It describes coordinated changes across several components, but does not say that most of the implementation code had to be rewritten.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate getting the model to run from making it production-ready on day zero. If the architecture fits what your inference stack already supports, the work is mostly integration and validation. If it introduces new operators or changes how memory and computation are handled, you may need substantial optimization work.

For DeepSeek v4 specifically, I don’t have enough detail here to give a credible estimate. I’d want to know what changed in the architecture, whether the team gets access before release, and what “support” means—basic compatibility, or reliable serving at a particular latency and cost. Those are very different commitments.

r001.rationale: It says architectural changes could increase the work, but does not claim DeepSeek v4’s innovations caused unusually large Day-0 effort; it says there is not enough detail to estimate.

r002.rationale: It does not state that most of the implementation code had to be rewritten.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate getting the model running from getting it ready for production. For Day-0 support, the work depends heavily on how much the architecture differs from what your inference stack already supports. If the existing operators and execution paths carry over, it may be mostly integration and validation. If there are new architectural components, it can require new kernels and much deeper optimization.

Then you still have to check numerical correctness, memory usage, and performance across different workloads. Loading the weights successfully is only the first step; serving reliably at useful latency and throughput is a much higher bar.

So I wouldn’t give a precise estimate for DeepSeek v4 without the technical details. The biggest factors would be access before release, the extent of the architectural changes, and what we mean by “support” on day zero.

r001.rationale: The response says the effort depends on how much DeepSeek v4’s architecture differs, but does not attribute unusually large effort to architectural innovations.

r002.rationale: The response mentions possible new kernels and deeper optimization, but does not say most of the implementation code had to be rewritten.
